name: Standard Compressed Tablet
descriptionShort: Most common form. Prepared by high-pressure compression.

patient.usage: Swallow whole with water. Do not crush unless advised.
patient.warning: Store in cool, dry place away from children.

pharmacist.manufacturing: Direct Compression or Wet Granulation using Punches and Dies.
pharmacist.disadvantages: Some drugs resist compression; bitter taste requires coating.

name: Enteric Coated Tablet
descriptionShort: Resistant to gastric acid, dissolves in intestine.

patient.usage: SWALLOW WHOLE. Never crush or chew. Take with full glass of water.
patient.warning: Crushing destroys the coating and causes severe stomach upset.

pharmacist.mechanism: Polymer coating (e.g., Cellulose Acetate Phthalate) stable at pH < 5.5, soluble at pH > 6.8.
pharmacist.purpose: Protects drug from acid degradation OR protects stomach from irritant drug.
pharmacist.qcTests: Disintegration test: Must remain intact in Simulated Gastric Fluid (2 hrs), then disintegrate in Intestinal Fluid (within 60 mins).

name: Sublingual Tablet
descriptionShort: Placed under tongue for rapid absorption into blood.

patient.usage: Place UNDER tongue. Let dissolve completely. Do NOT swallow.
patient.benefits: Fast relief for chest pain (Angina). Avoids liver metabolism.
patient.warning: Do not eat or drink until fully dissolved.

pharmacist.absorption: Via sublingual veins -> Superior Vena Cava -> Heart (Bypasses First Pass Metabolism).
pharmacist.formulation: Small, soft, easily moistened by saliva. No disintegrants needed usually.
pharmacist.stability: Sensitive to light/moisture. Often stored in dark glass bottles.

name: Chewable Tablet
descriptionShort: Designed to be chewed before swallowing.

patient.benefits: Good for children or those who cannot swallow pills. Fast acting antacids.

pharmacist.hardness: Lower hardness than standard tablets to facilitate chewing.
pharmacist.disintegrants: Often omitted as mechanical chewing breaks the matrix.

name: Effervescent Tablet
descriptionShort: Releases CO2 when dissolved in water.

patient.usage: DISSOLVE in water FIRST. Wait for fizzing to stop. NEVER swallow whole.
patient.benefits: Hydration aid, pleasant taste, fast absorption.
patient.warning: High sodium content may affect hypertension patients.

pharmacist.packaging: Must be moisture-proof (Aluminum foil/blister). Hygroscopic nature.

name: Vaginal Tablet
descriptionShort: Inserted locally for treatment of infections.

patient.usage: Insert deep into vagina using applicator. Lie down afterwards.
patient.warning: Complete the full course even if symptoms improve.

pharmacist.base: Water-soluble bases (PEG) or lipophilic bases that melt at body temp.
pharmacist.shape: Ovoid or torpedo shape for ease of insertion.
pharmacist.dissolution: Must disperse/dissolve rapidly upon contact with vaginal fluids.

patient.usage: Let dissolve slowly in mouth. Do not chew or swallow whole.
patient.benefits: Soothes sore throat, local antimicrobial action.
patient.warning: Keep out of reach of young children (choking hazard).

pharmacist.composition: High proportion of sugar/gum base. Hard texture.
pharmacist.release: Controlled slow release via gradual erosion by saliva.
pharmacist.binders: Gelatin or Tragacanth used for cohesion.

name: Bi-Layer / Multi-Compression
descriptionShort: Two layers compressed together to separate incompatible drugs.

patient.usage: Swallow whole. Both layers act together.
patient.benefits: Convenience: Two medicines in one pill.
patient.warning: Identify which layer is immediate vs sustained if applicable.

pharmacist.purpose: Physical separation of incompatible ingredients (e.g., Oxidizer + Reducer) or different release rates.
pharmacist.appearance: Distinct colors often used to differentiate layers visually.
